results.title: Alteration of the structural properties of inulin gels
results.content:
## 1. Introduction


Inulin is a well-known oligosaccharide which can be easily extracted from several economically important plants, such as chicory, onion, garlic and wheat. Inulin belongs chemically to the family of the fructans, built up of 2 -90 β-(2,1) linked fructose units and, most often, a terminal glucose molecule [1]. The inulin molecule's average degree of polymerization is dependent on the source it is extracted from. The distribution of the chain lengths is relatively broad and ranges from the monosaccharide fructose up to chains composing of 90 fructose units. Nutritionally it is used as a dietary fiber and exhibits low calorie content, prebiotic properties and is suitable for diabetic nutrition [2,3]. Inulin/water suspensions can form particle gels with a fat like structure [4,5]. Such extraordinary mechanical properties suggest outstanding and basic physical properties. Depending on the inulin molecule's degree of polymerization, nowadays inulin is commercially used as sugar replacement (low DP), texturizer (medium DP) and as fat replacer (high DP). These days consumers are becoming more and more health-conscious and emphasize a healthy nutrition [6][7][8].

Regarding this trend, this work is focused on the basic physical properties and the development of a consistent model, explaining the gel formation of inulin with a high DP and providing a better understanding for its potential as fat replacer in fat containing food.

### 1.1 The particle gel model


In this section, the formation of an inulin particle gel is introduced. The model consist of an adaption of previous publications [9] and our personal findings.

When a certain amount of polydisperse (broad chain length distribution) long chain (average DP = 23) inulin is added to water, the dissolved amount depends on the temperature of the solvent and the chain lengths of the inulin molecules (Fig. 1). Naturally short, low molecular weight chains dissolve faster and at lower temperatures, compared to long, high molecular weight chains (this is due to the change in the Gibbs free energy of a solute/solvent mixture , which ∆𝐺 𝑀 decreases with decreasing DP of the solute, see [10]). The dissolved polydisperse oligosaccharides can be approximately visualized by (semi flexible) rods of different lengths [11]. Upon cooling, the dissolved inulin molecules recrystallize selectively, driven by chain length and temperature. In addition, to start the crystallization process, crystallization nuclei are necessary. In the present case, undissolved material acts as "seeds" which enable a relative fast recrystallization process. On the contrary, if the complete amount of inulin is dissolved, e.g. at sufficiently high temperatures, a particle gel as proposed in Fig. 1 will not be formed during cooling [12]. The molecules with a larger DP recrystallize first, forming nuclei (due to the lower solubility in water and thermodynamic fluctuations), and the molecules with a smaller DP accumulate on the outer regions of the developing crystallites. When the crystallization process continues, the inulin crystallites form aggregates (acting as primary particles in the particle gel network). Those are characterized by very strong interactions due to their crystallization energy, when different crystallites interact via their crystalline surfaces. However, these processes happen at random places throughout the entire sample. When the gel formation continues, the primary particles form clusters of random, irregular, perhaps fractal nature, which are mainly attracted to each other by van der Waals forces [12]. Moreover, when these random clusters meet at larger scales, a particle network is formed, which defines most of the structural and mechanical properties of the macroscopic sample. The water is trapped in the meshes and interspaces of the particle gel [9]. For varying types of inulin, differing in their average DP, the particle gel network also varies in packing density and gel particle size. Those variations have a significant impact on the physical properties of the completely developed inulin gels, illustrating once more the varying texture of inulin gels prepared with different types of inulin. At the current state, it needs to be stressed, that this model is not proven in all details.

## Materials and Methods


### 2.1 Materials


All the samples were prepared with a type of long chain Inulin (average DP = 23).

It is commercially sold as spray dried, colorless powder by Beneo, Belgium.

### 2.2 Sample preparation and Analytical methods


All samples had been prepared as inulin/water suspensions, containing 20% (w/w) inulin dry matter. The standard sample preparation was identical for all analysis methods. The suspensions were prepared by adding the inulin powder in portions under constant stirring (600 rpm/7000 rpm) to the respective amount of deionized water, which had been heated to the desired sample preparation temperatures (25,40 and 60 °C) in advance. The suspension was stirred at the desired temperature for 10 min in a sealed beaker, to minimize water loss during heating. This suspension was processed accordingly to the intended analysis method.

To better understand the impact of a higher shear rate (7000 rpm, IKA Ultra Turrax T18) during sample preparation, on the gel hardness and the particle size of the inulin gels, the gels were also prepared as samples with a high shear rate applied during sample preparation (the suspensions were prepared as mentioned above with a shear rate of 7000 rpm instead of 600 rpm). Those suspensions were prepared for the texture analysis (section 2.2.4) and for the particle size determination (section 2.2.5). Apart from those exceptions, all the samples were only prepared with a shear rate of 600 rpm.

#### 2.2.1 Solubility in water


To determine the solubility of 20% inulin in deionized water (i.e. 10 g inulin in 40 g water), a sample was taken from the above mentioned suspension after 10 min stirring at the desired sample preparation temperature. The undissolved inulin and the solution were separated from each other by centrifugation (14100 xg, 2 min, using a table centrifuge MiniSpin by Eppendorf). The refractive index of the inulin solution at 20 °C was measured, using a digital refractometer

#### 2.2.2 X-ray diffraction


The crystallinity of spray dried inulin powder and developing inulin gels, was determined by X-ray diffraction (XRD). Measurements were done at a selfconstructed instrument using a rotating anode x-ray generator (Rigaku MicroMax 007), multilayer optics (Osmic Confocal Max-Flux, Cu -K α , λ = 1.54 Å) and a 2D online image plate detector (Mar345). The samples were contained in quartz glass capillaries (length = 80 mm, outer diameter = 1.5 mm, wall thickness = 0.01 mm) and measured in transmission geometry for scattering angles 2θ between 5° and 25°.Diffraction patterns were obtained by radial averaging of the 2D data. To obtain the powder diffractograms, the samples were exposed for 10 minutes. For the in-situ XRD experiments during gel formation, inulin suspensions were examined every 5 min over an aging time of 24 h.

#### 2.2.3 High Performance Anion Exchange Chromatography (HPAEC)


To examine how the chain length distribution of the inulin depends on the gel preparation temperature, HPAEC was performed. A sample was taken from the inulin suspension (section 2.2), after 10 minutes of stirring at the desired preparation temperature. The remainder of the suspension was decanted into disposable vessels (d = 27 mm; h = 42 mm), sealed airtight and another sample was taken after 24 h of quiescent storage at room temperature. For both samples, the undissolved inulin and the solution were separated from each other by centrifugation (14800 rpm, 2 min) and the overlapping solution was diluted 1:20 with deionized water. Of this dilution 10 µL were injected into the ICS -5000+ DC by Dionex and separated on a CarboPac PA200 IC column, with a gradient of 120 -320 mM sodium acetate in 100 mM sodium hydroxid, using a constant eluent flow of 0.5 mL/min. The separated fractions were detected by a pulsed amperometric detector (PAD).

#### 2.2.4 Texture analysis


For the texture analysis of the inulin gels, two different methods were performed. To determine the distinctive crack pattern of the samples, the inulin suspension, described in section 2.2, was stored in cylindrical shaped Teflon vessels (d = 40 mm; h = 30 mm) and sealed airtight. After 24 h storing at room temperature, the samples were removed from the vessels and measured with the Z005 AllroundLine texture analyzer by Zwick Roell. The setup of the texture analyzer was a cylindrical shaped stainless steel stamp (d = 7 cm), that compressed the sample to a maximum strain of 6 mm with a constant speed of 0.2 mm/s. To measure the gel hardness, the above mentioned inulin suspension was stored in disposable vessels as described in section 2.2.3 and measured after 24 h with the Z005 AllroundLine texture analyzer by Zwick Roell. The setup of the texture analyzer was a cylindrical shaped stainless steel stamp (d = 1 cm), that penetrated the sample 6 mm deep with a constant speed of 0.2 mm/s. To determine a reproducible zero point, a trigger force of 0.1 N was set.

#### 2.2.5 Particle size determination (Light scattering)


To perform the particle size analysis, the inulin suspension was processed as described in section 2.2.3. The inulin gel (24 h age) was diluted 1:20 with a 1:1 sucrose/water solution. To disperse the gel primary particles, the diluted inulin suspension was treated with ultrasound for 1 min, with the amplitude set to 75% using the UIP1000hd ultrasonic rod (d (Sonotrode) = 22 mm) by Hielscher. To remove remaining aggregates, the treated sample was filtered through a filter with 4 -7 µm pore size. The filtrate was analyzed by static light scattering using the LS13320 laser diffraction particle size analyzer by Beckmann Coulter. To determine the particle size distribution of the inulin primary particles, an optical model had to be formulated, which requires the complex refractive index as input parameter. For the real part of the refractive index 1.52 was used [13]. It is also known, that the refractive index of inulin is only marginally influenced by differences in molecular weight [9]. So the above mentioned real part of the refractive index could be used for high DP inulin and also for other types of inulin.

Since the imaginary part of the complex refractive index of inulin is unknown, it was set to 0.1 according to the guidelines of Beckmann Coulter [14]. To minimize the influence of inulin aggregates, that passed the pores of the round filter or reaggregated after filtration, the arithmetic mean diameter ( ) of the inulin 𝐷10 primary particles was analyzed.

## Results and Discussion


### 3.1 X-ray powder diffraction


The x-ray powder diffraction was performed with the untreated inulin powder provided by Beneo. The resulting pattern is represented in Fig. 2. The sample yields an amorphous halo. No Bragg reflexes were found between 2θ = 5° -25°.

### 3.2 Solubility


The solubility of inulin in water was already examined previously to this work (e.g. [12]). In those previously published manuscripts, the authors just focus on the saturation concentration of inulin at the respective temperature, without taking into account the polydispersity of inulin, which has a significant impact on As mentioned above, with an increasing total amount of inulin added to water, the amount of dissolved inulin increases too. Since the sample, with an added amount of 30% (w/w) of inulin, formed very hard gels, even after 10 minutes sample preparation, the dry matter and the liquid phase could not be separated properly from each other by centrifugation and no values for this concentration could be obtained. As all samples in this work were prepared with 20% dry matter of inulin, here the solubility of inulin at different sample preparation temperatures also refers to 20% dry matter in the sample. The equilibrium solubility in deionized water is shown in Fig. 5. To determine the concentration of dissolved inulin, a reference curve was generated, by examination of the refractive indices at specific mass concentrations of inulin dissolved in deionized water. The measured indices were plotted against the mass concentration of inulin and fitted with a linear fit. The data has been fitted over the concentration range 0 ≤ c ≤ 0.35 and the equation of the linear fit can be found in Fig. 4. The solubility of inulin increases with increasing sample preparation temperature. The mostly amorphous inulin powder can be dissolved in a relative large amount with a comparatively small thermal energy input. This is why almost 90% of the total amount is already dissolved at 25 °C preparation temperature. The maximum solubility of 20% of inulin dry matter is reached at temperatures slightly above 60 °C. Since the total amount of added inulin was 20%, even at increased preparation temperatures the dissolved amount will remain the same.

### 3.3 X-ray diffraction during gelation


In previously published manuscripts, the physical parameters of inulin powder [15] and also the crystal structure of the inulin particles [16] have been examined by small and wide angle x-ray scattering (SAXS and WAXS). In this work a WAXS approach was chosen, to examine the crystallization kinetics of inulin during gel formation. Therefore, in this work the focus is on the determination of the crystallization speed by application of the Avrami model. The development of the particle gel network was examined by in-situ x-ray diffraction. Radial averaged diffraction patterns of an inulin gel, prepared at 25 °C with a stirring rate of 600 rpm and measured for 24 h during gelation, can be seen in Fig. 6. With increasing aging time, the Bragg intensities of the samples increase. The integrated intensities of the Bragg reflections quantitatively represent the increasing crystallinity of the developing particle gel network [17], with increasing sample age. Taking into account that the spray dried inulin powder is mostly amorphous (Fig. 2), this result confirms that the dissolved inulin partly crystallizes during gelation (see section 1.1). The intensities of the Bragg reflexes at 2θ = 12.1° had been projected to the left hand layer, to make the gelation process more obvious. To examine the crystallization kinetics of the gel formation, the 12.1° reflexes were integrated and normalized to the final values observed after 24 h. In Fig. 7 the relative intensities of the Bragg reflexes at 2θ = 12.1° of inulin gels, prepared at 25 °C, 40 °C and 60 °C (shear rate 600 rpm), are compared to each other. For all samples, the predominant fraction of the crystalline material forms within the first two to three hours of the gelation. In those first hours, the intensity increases to 80 -85% of the maximum intensity. This rapid increase of the intensity is due to the fast initial crystallization process of the inulin particles. In the immediate phase of the crystallization, the system exhibits a very high crystallization rate, due to the presence of many seeds and the high concentration of dissolved inulin chains, i.e., a large amount of crystallizable material. Since the seeds are randomly distributed throughout the entire sample, the crystallization will proceed quickly. In this initial phase, mostly the primary particle formation occurs. When the crystallization progresses further, the system achieves a state of low Gibbs free energy, the main part of the primary particles is already formed (meaning the main part of the crystallizable material is already crystallized) and the crystallization rate decreases significantly. This can be observed in Fig. 7 of the gel formation, a Johnson -Mehl -Avrami -Kolmogorov fit (JMAK) was 𝑘 applied to the curves shown in Fig. 7. The JMAK model attempts to describe an isothermal phase transition [18] semi-phenomenologically, in this case the transition from liquid to crystalline. The respective equation can be seen in Eq.( 1). in those situations is continually changing. This non-integer values for also 𝑚 𝑚 occur for the crystallization of inulin gels and can arise from the above mentioned processes (see also section 1.1). Therefore, in this work the focus of the examination of the crystallization kinetics was set on the determination of the constant . The crystallization constant decreases with increasing preparation 𝑘 temperature. With increasing temperature the solubility also increases (Fig. 5) and with it the amount of nuclei, which act as seeding material, decreases. This results in a decreased crystallization rate. The decreased crystallization rate influences the average gel particle size, altering the texture of the completely developed inulin gel significantly. Those results will be explained in the following sections.

### 3.4 High Performance Anion Exchange Chromatography (HPAEC)


To determine the chain length distribution of the initially dissolved inulin, one sample was taken from the inulin suspension (20% inulin dry matter) after 10 min stirring at the respective preparation temperature. Another one was taken from the same gel after 24 h storage at room temperature, to determine the amount of inulin remaining dissolved. Both samples were diluted with deionized water and analyzed by HPAEC. To determine the DP distribution of the samples, a reference value was prepared by completely dissolving 20% dry matter of inulin in deionized water at 85 °C. The obtained chromatogram can be seen in Fig. 8. The peaks in Fig. 8 are indicated with the respective DP. The first peak identified is the DP-6 peak, meaning one glucose head group bound to a chain of five β -(2,1) linked fructose units. Molecules with a smaller DP could not be completely separated from each other, represented by the large peak at 2 min retention time, originating from the application of the CarboPac PA200 column, which is mainly used for the separation of oligosaccharides. To figure out the amount of inulin of a certain DP, dissolved during sample preparation, the areas below the peaks in the chromatogram were integrated. To point out changes in the DP distribution of the dissolved inulin and to minimize concentration errors, resulting from the sample preparation, a region of ten following DPs was summed up to one fraction. The results can be seen in Fig. 9. With increasing sample preparation temperature, the amount of dissolved inulin also increases. Compared to the reference values, even at 60 °C preparation temperature a small amount of inulin remains undissolved, ensuring a seedinduced crystallization during gel formation. As already mentioned in section 1.1, a seeded crystallization is inevitable for the formation of a completely percolated inulin gel. With increasing solubility, the amount of dissolved long chain inulin (DP 36 -85) also significantly increases. To determine the DP distribution of the inulin, remaining dissolved after 24 h of storage at room temperature, the 24 h samples were analyzed accordingly to the 10 min samples, as already explained earlier in this section. The results are shown in Fig. 10. Comparing the results from Fig. 9 and Fig. 10 it can be seen clearly that the previously dissolved inulin almost completely recrystallizes during gel formation. Only a small amount of short chain inulin, increasing with increasing preparation temperature, remains dissolved after 24 h. Above a DP of 35 the dissolved inulin completely crystallizes. Referring to the DP distribution of the gel primary particles, which are formed during crystallization (see section 1.1), an increased sample preparation temperature leads to the incorporation of a larger amount of long chain inulin in those particles. This influences the primary particle size and with it the texture of the completely developed inulin gel (see sections 3.5 and 3.6).

### 3.5 Deformation, facture and texture analysis


The gel hardness of inulin gels with a dry matter content of 20% (w/w) has already been determined previously to this work with similar analysis methods (e.g. [19]). In this work the hardness of the completely developed inulin gels is examined according to the sample preparation temperature and the respective primary particle size (see section 3.6). Therefore, the gel hardness has been examined once again, based on the current research topic.

To learn about the fracture behavior of the completely developed inulin gels, the samples were compressed beyond their fracture stress. In Fig. 11 the reader can see two samples after compression, prepared at different sample preparation temperatures. The gel in Fig. 11 A was prepared at 25 °C. It shows a distinctive crack pattern, which shows "slip bands", which are often observed in fragile solids. This is a typical behavior for a strong gel [20]. When the inulin sample is compressed uniaxial, the upper and lower parts of the sample are compressed in the direction of the applied force and the outside parts are forced sideways. For this fracture behavior, the gel needs a certain stiffness, which arises from the binding forces between the particles in the gel. If the bonds between the particles of the gel get weaker, this crack pattern disappears and at larger strains the gels begin to yield and flow instead of fracturing [20]. This behavior can be observed for an inulin gel, prepared at 60 °C (Fig. 11 B). Therefore, the fracture behavior of the inulin gels proposes a strong hint of the influence of the different sample preparation temperatures on the hardness of the gels.

To examine the hardness of the inulin gels, the samples were penetrated by a stainless steel stamp to a maximum strain of 6 mm. The responsive force was measured and the resulting gel hardness could be determined, as the first maximum of the force versus strain curve before the fracturing of the gel [21].

The results of the hardness measurements of the inulin gels, prepared at different sample preparation temperatures and with low (600 rpm) and high (7000 rpm) shear rates, are pictured in Fig. 12. One can observe the hardness of the inulin gels decrease with increasing sample preparation temperature. The application of a higher shear rate (7000 rpm) during sample preparation, results in increased hardness values, whereas the hardness trends for low and high shear rates remain identical throughout the whole temperature range. The explanation for those trends will be given in the following sections. At even higher sample preparation temperatures, above a 60 °C, the formation of inulin gels cannot be observed, due to its high solubility in water. At these preparation conditions, more than 20% of inulin are dissolved, which leads to an unseeded crystallization upon cooling and results in a fragmentary gel structure.

So the mechanical properties of the developing inulin gels can be influenced by the variation of shear rate and temperature during sample preparation.

### 3.6 Particle size


The particle size trends of the inulin gels provide an explanation for the above discussed hardness trends and can be observed in Fig. 13. The average size of the inulin gel primary particles, prepared at low and high shear rates, increases with increasing sample preparation temperature. This is due to the increasing solubility of inulin in water at higher sample preparation temperatures and the depletion of seeding material connected therewith [9]. Since all samples are cooled to room temperature for crystallization and all samples contain 20% of inulin dry matter, the amount of crystallizable material is comparable in all the samples. With increasing sample preparation temperature, the amount of seeding material, which is left in the inulin suspension, decreases, resulting in a decreasing crystallization constant (see section 3.3). Additionally, a larger 𝑘 amount of long chain inulin is dissolved at increased preparation temperatures.

As already seen in section 3.4, above a DP of 35, the previously dissolved inulin completely recrystallizes upon gel formation. This results in the incorporation of a larger amount of long chain inulin in the gel primary particles of the inulin gels, prepared at higher temperatures. So the decreasing crystallization constant and the incorporation of a larger amount of long chain inulin at increased preparation temperatures, cause the formation of larger and less numerous crystalline gel primary particles. Those larger gel particles are also responsible for the decreased hardness of the inulin gels [12] at increased sample preparation temperatures (see Fig. 12). The gel primary particles are assumably spherical shaped. Compared to smaller spherical particles, the surface to volume ratio of larger spherical particles is smaller. In consequence, the larger particles can form fewer bonds between each other and the inulin gel hardness decreases with increasing sample preparation temperature. Another obvious trend is the smaller particle size for inulin gels, prepared with high shear rates (7000 rpm). The mostly amorphous inulin powder, depending on the amount of inulin and the temperature, partly dissolves in water. The undissolved material can act as seeding material upon cooling. If the shear rate during sample preparation is significantly increased (comparing 600 rpm and 7000 rpm), the undissolved material is much better dispersed and eventually numerous seeds are broken apart and therefore reduced in size [22]. This results in smaller and more numerous gel primary particles. Those smaller particles yield gels with increased hardness (see Fig. 12). The reason for this is again the larger surface to volume ratio of smaller spherical particles and the additional bonds, which can be established between those primary particles. So the inulin gel properties depend delicately on the gel primary particle size. To state the impact of the particle size on the gel hardness once again, in Fig. 14 the hardness of the completely developed inulin gels, prepared with a stirring rate of 600 rpm and 7000 rpm at increasing sample preparation temperatures, is plotted against the respective primary particle size. As already mentioned above, the hardness decreases with increasing particle size. Within the error limits, the hardness of the high and low shear rate gels at identical primary particle sizes, corresponds to each other.

### 3.7 Particle gels as fractal clusters


In this subsection the fractal nature of the networks is suggested, analogously to fat crystal networks, which are supposed to exhibit a fractal structure [23]. The nature of the crystallization process in fats and inulin have definitely many similarities, despite fats are composed of triacylglycerols. Nevertheless, the crystallization of fats is also selective, due to varying chain lengths and their saturation degree, which determines the polymorphs and crystallization defects inside the primary particles. The large scale properties look quite similar [24].

The fractal dimension of the fat crystal network gives information about its 𝐷 𝑓 structure and can be determined by various methods such as light microscopy (Fractal Box counting) and the determination of the solid and the liquid fraction of fats [23,25,26] In this paper we introduce another method using rheological measurements of amplitude sweeps and their interpretation using a Kraus type model [23,27,28], where the breakdown of the structure can be related to the applied shear amplitude. This approach turns out to be more effective for (fractal) inulin particle gels.

To understand those ideas on a more quantitative basis, we summarize the basic notations used in the following sections of the paper. The information in this section was mostly taken from references [23], [20] and [29].

The essential property of a fractal object is its "scale invariance", meaning it is "self-similar". Therefore, if an ideal fractal structure is subdivided into smaller structures, each subset will contain scaled down versions of the whole object.

Many natural objects, such as trees, coastlines or the vascular system, exhibit fractal properties. To describe those fractal objects in a mathematical way, the Euclidian or Newtonian dimensionality, which is clearly defined in three dimensions, is not sufficient any more. Since fractal objects exhibit an irregular structure, they cannot be described by an integer, but rather a fractal dimension

. If an object can be subdivided into copies of itself with scaling factor , 𝐷 𝑓 𝑁 𝑓 then its fractal dimension can be determined by Eq.( 2).

Eq.( 2) applies very well for objects, which contain exact subcopies of themselves (ideal fractals). The fractal dimension of particle gels cannot be determined that easy. As already mentioned in section 1.1, the inulin particle gels consist of inulin primary particles, which aggregate under quiescent conditions. The aggregation of spherical particles at rest leads to clusters with a fractal structure [20]. The inulin particle gels consist of colloidal clusters with an average random fractal structure on certain length scales and exhibit no exact self-similarity, as known from "mathematical fractals [30].

Nevertheless the irregular, fractal network structure is responsible for the viscoelastic response of the inulin gels [31], which can be measured by oscillation rheology. Above a certain shear amplitude, the inulin gels show a strong and well defined shear thinning behavior [31]. This behavior suggests the comparison of the inulin particle network to a filler particle network consisting of carbon black particles, as often used in rubber compounds [28]. The rheological behavior under deformation of those network types is described by the "Payne effect", which can be quantified by applying the "Kraus model" on amplitude sweep curves, obtained by rheological measurements [27]. The respective Equation can be seen in Eq.( 3).

## 4. Summary


Taking the above discussed results into account, the preparation temperature dependent hardness variation of the completely developed inulin gels can be summarized by a simple model. The model is pictured in Fig. 16. In Fig. 16 one can see the particle gel structures of two completely developed inulin gels, one prepared at 25 °C and one prepared at 60 °C. Since the model in Fig. 16 is simplified and intended to illustrate the temperature dependent particle size variation, the pictured dimensions are randomly chosen. For the gel prepared at 25 °C, a sufficient amount of inulin remains undissolved during sample preparation and acts as crystallization nuclei, ensuring a seeded crystallization. After 24 h of crystallization, the resulting gel consists of small primary particles and exhibits a hard texture. If the preparation temperature is increased to 60 °C, the solubility of the inulin in water also significantly increases and with it the amount of undissolved nuclei decreases. This causes a considerable decrease in crystallization velocity. Additionally, a larger amount of long chain inulin is incorporated in the crystallizing gel primary particles. The resulting gel consists of fewer but larger particles and exhibits a remarkably decreased hardness. In consequence, these physical ideas of the structure 556 behavior relationship of particle gels can be used to control the texture of inulin 557 containing food systems much better.
